query: Consider a single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy subjected to uniaxial tensile loading in the elastic-to-plastic transition regime. The material exhibits a yield strength that appears anomalously insensitive to strain rates compared to traditional metals, despite high strain rates leading to significant dislocation accumulation. The operating regime includes temperatures ranging from cryogenic to elevated (up to 600 K). What is the dominant mechanism driving the onset of yielding (e.g., dislocation nucleation at specific defects vs. thermal activation)? Identify the design constraints regarding crystal orientation anisotropy and propose a boundary condition test to falsify the hypothesis that FCC-to-BCC phase transformation is the primary deformation mode.

generation.hypothesis: In single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloys (HEAs) within the elastic-to-plastic transition regime, the onset of yielding is dominated by thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide, rather than phase transformation. The anomalously low strain-rate sensitivity arises from the high lattice distortion and chemical short-range order (CSRO) in the FCC matrix, which creates a high density of local energy barriers that are overcome by thermal fluctuations, making the yield stress less dependent on strain rate compared to traditional metals. The primary deformation mechanism involves the nucleation of partial dislocations at surface defects or pre-existing dislocation sources, followed by twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and martensitic transformation to HCP phase at cryogenic temperatures, while at elevated temperatures (up to 600 K), thermal activation facilitates dislocation unlocking from Lomer-Cottrell locks, maintaining ductility. Crystal orientation anisotropy imposes a design constraint where the <001> direction exhibits the highest yield strength due to the FCC slip system geometry, while <111> and <101> orientations show lower yield strengths and higher anisotropy in deformation behavior. A boundary condition test to falsify the FCC-to-BCC phase transformation hypothesis involves conducting in-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HT-XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) on single-crystal specimens under uniaxial tensile loading at 600 K; if no BCC phase peaks or BCC lattice signatures are detected during yielding and plastic deformation, the hypothesis that FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode is falsified.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-crystal FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy with FCC crystal structure, compositional homogeneity, and low initial dislocation density.
generation.intervention: Uniaxial tensile loading applied across strain rates from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 at temperatures ranging from 77 K to 600 K.
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 77 K to 600 K; Strain rates: 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1; Crystal orientation: <001>, <111>, and <101> directions tested.
generation.structural_mediator: Chemical short-range order (CSRO) and lattice distortion in the FCC matrix, which modulate dislocation nucleation barriers and glide mobility.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated dislocation nucleation and glide, with twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) and martensitic transformation to HCP phase at low temperatures; at high temperatures, thermal activation unlocks Lomer-Cottrell locks, enabling continued plasticity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Yield strength will show minimal dependence on strain rate due to thermal activation overcoming local energy barriers. Deformation will be dominated by partial dislocation nucleation, twinning, and HCP phase formation at low temperatures, while at high temperatures, dislocation slip and HCP phase accumulation will dominate. No BCC phase transformation will be observed.
generation.baseline: Traditional metals with FCC structure (e.g., pure Ni, Cu) exhibit higher strain-rate sensitivity in yield strength due to lower lattice distortion and absence of CSRO.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds for single-crystal FCC FeNiCrMn HEAs; it may not apply to polycrystalline or BCC-structured HEAs, or to temperatures above 600 K where phase instability might occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact contribution of CSRO to dislocation nucleation barriers is not fully quantified, and the role of surface defects in nucleation may vary with specimen preparation. The transition temperature between TWIP and dislocation-dominated mechanisms may depend on specific alloy composition and processing history.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform in-situ HT-XRD and TEM on single-crystal FeNiCrMn HEA specimens under uniaxial tensile loading at 600 K. If no BCC phase peaks or BCC lattice signatures are detected during yielding and plastic deformation, the hypothesis that FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode is falsified.

Microstructure of selective laser-melted equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy

Figure 1 shows an SEM-BSE image and EDS mapping results of as-built equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. The BSE image revealed some micron-scale gas pores, but coarse defects or cracks were not observed in the as-built HEA (Porosity: 0.13%). The density of the present alloy was measured as 7.96 g/cm 3 which was similar to that of the theoretical density of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA. In addition, Co, Cr, Fe, Mn, and Ni were all around 20 at. % in EDS mapping analysis, and all elements were evenly distributed. Li et al . [38] found that Mn undergoes segregation when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA is manufactured using SLM. According to Wang et al . [41] , when equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA was manufactured with pre-alloyed powder using electron beam melting (EBM), it was confirmed that Fe, Cr and Co elements segregate into the dendrite, whereas, Mn and Ni segregate into the interdendrite region. However, when the optimal process condition using SLM was deduced, no dendritic microstructure was formed, and it was possible to manufacture a random solid solution HEA with compositional homogeneity.

3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs

Figure 2 shows the stress–strain curves of the Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs at 77, 300, and 1000 K respectively. At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. The phase transformation is mainly driven by the surface stresses which enable the reduction in surface energy in the nanowire. On further loading, the difference between two boundaries decreases and finally vanishes at around 50% elongation, resulting in an improved work hardening.
